Dermatology · published research

Venous ulcer

Some small controlled studies report faster healing with selected red or near-infrared protocols. However, a 2026 meta-analysis found no statistically significant overall reduction in ulcer area, and results varied substantially among trials.

PBM Database summary

What the records report

Some small controlled studies report faster healing with selected red or near-infrared protocols. However, a 2026 meta-analysis found no statistically significant overall reduction in ulcer area, and results varied substantially among trials.

Summary of the Evidence

Twenty-seven exact-category titles include 23 primary human reports, three reviews or meta-analyses, and one protocol. Two 2005 papers are duplicate reports from the same 44-person randomized trial, leaving at most 22 independent primary cohorts; overlap between two Gupta reports from 1997 and 1998 is uncertain. The 2026 meta-analysis includes eleven randomized trials and reuses some of these primary reports, so its participants should not be added again to the database publication count.

Human and clinical evidence

Results are mixed. A double-blind placebo-controlled trial of 20 people with 32 chronic ulcers tested combined 660-nm red and 890-nm near-infrared LED. The authors reported faster healing in the light-treated groups at several follow-up visits, including differences from placebo by days 30 and 90 (Caetano et al. 2009). Other small trials reported improvements in some wound measures, while sham-controlled studies also found no clear advantage or uncertain effects.

The 2026 systematic review included 11 randomized trials, with 615 participants randomized overall and 340 participants with venous ulcers. Four trials could be pooled for ulcer-area change. The pooled difference was not statistically significant, and heterogeneity was high. All included trials raised some or high risk-of-bias concerns. This does not erase positive results in individual trials, but it means the overall area-reduction effect has not been established (Rasul et al. 2026).

A retrospective study reported shorter healing time with light plus traditional dressings, and small case series describe closure during blue-light treatment. These observations are useful clinically but cannot isolate light from compression, debridement, dressings, vascular care, or selection of wounds likely to heal. One trial using water-filtered infrared included substantial heating and should not be treated as equivalent to nonthermal PBM.

Animal evidence

No animal study directly addressing venous ulcers was identified in the exact category.

In-vitro and ex-vivo evidence

No venous-ulcer-specific cell or ex-vivo study was identified in the exact category.

Treatment Parameters and Generalizability

Clinical reports include red visible LED around 625–685 nm, often at roughly 3–4 J/cm², and near-infrared light around 810–980 nm with much wider reported fluences. Schedules range from once weekly to several sessions per week. Devices, wound preparation, compression, and standard care differ. Some high-fluence or heated-light regimens are not directly comparable with nonthermal PBM, and the trials do not establish one preferred dose.

Interpretation

The evidence contains favorable findings from selected small trials, alongside null or uncertain comparisons. The largest synthesis available here did not show a statistically significant overall reduction in ulcer area. PBM may have a role as an adjunct under particular protocols, but the average benefit and the best regimen remain unclear.

Evidence strength in source summaryLow for faster healing under some specific red or near-infrared protocols Low for overall ulcer-area reduction across PBM protocols
Publications and records27 articles

Evidence strength rationale and next steps

Some small controlled trials report faster healing or area reduction, while other trials are null or uncertain. A 2026 review pooled four trials and found no statistically significant overall reduction in ulcer area, with very high heterogeneity. A larger masked trial using consistent compression care, clearly reported light dosing, and common healing outcomes would help determine which protocols, if any, add benefit.
